newsitem.title: USA: Israeli calls for end to terrorism before talks.
newsitem.headline: Israeli calls for end to terrorism before talks.

text.p: Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechi told U.S. leaders on Thursday that Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat must clamp down on terrorism and violence as a precondition for resuming peace talks.

"I clarified again that what is necessary now (is) that Chairman Arafat orders his commanders and his security forces to fight against terrorism," he told reporters after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
"When he starts to do that we can come back, have a discussion with the Palestinians. There are a lot of subjects ... that we need to move forward with them."
Mordechai was visiting Washington as the Clinton administration engaged in a new round of contacts to try to halt an escalation of Israeli-Palestinian violence and revive the crumbling peace process.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due in the U.S. capital on Monday to meet President Bill Clinton.

Negotiations have been derailed by Israel's decision to build new housing for Jews in East Jerusalem, which has provoked Arab outrage and U.S. criticism. Violent clashes and bombings have occurred in the Gaza strip and West Bank.

Mordechai, speaking earlier before talks with U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, made clear that Israel had no intention of quickly halting settlement work, especially construction of new housing in East Jerusalem.

When asked if the work might be halted in order to stop bombings and rock-throwing, he said: "I think we have our right to keep Jerusalem united for the Israeli people and for the Palestinians who are living there."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright and Mordechai, during an hour-long discussion, "did explore some specific ideas" for resuming peace talks. He refused to give details.

U.S. officials, however, described as premature Israeli media reports that Washington had decided on a Camp David-style negotiating marathon like the one that brought peace between Israel and Egypt in 1978.
"We haven't decided on anything yet. We're at the sifting-through stage," one official said.
Burns said Albright had pressed Mordechai for information on reports that Israel was "thickening" some of its existing settlements in the West Bank by building new housing.
He said the U.S. position was that such moves "create tensions and they're unhelpful in the peace negotiations."

But at an earlier news briefing Burns called on the Palestinian authority to "make very clear to its population and to all groups operating in Gaza and the West Bank that violence is not the answer, that terrorism is not the answer."
He urged both Israel and the Palestinians to avoid entrenched positions.

They should "be flexible in looking at ways to overcome their present differences" and not "embed themselves so deeply in rhetoric that they forget what the major objective here is, and that they are negotiating partners," he said.
Clinton, who met this week in Washington with Jordan's King Hussein, has said that he is willing to make considerable personal effort to rescue the peace process.
Netanyahu is due to meet Hussein on Sunday night in Minnesota, where the Jordanian monarch is undergoing surgery.

After the Mordechai-Cohen talks, the Pentagon said the United States had offered more financial aid to help Israel speed development of an anti-missile defence, including extra funds for the Arrow missile and a high-energy laser weapon.
Spokesman Ken Bacon said current U.S. aid of around $200 million over five years for the Arrow programme might be boosted by up to 25 per cent after consultation with Congress.
